title: The whirlpool ahead
hookLine: a man swept downstream, warned by someone on the bank

lines: A LAZY RIVER, A SUMMER AFTERNOON.
cards: A lazy river on a summer afternoon. Warm water, sun overhead, the current doing all the work. Nobody in the water has to decide anything.
That's the picture at the start of a teaching near the end of the Itivuttaka. A man is being carried along by a river that looks lovely and pleasant. He's enjoying it.
And then someone standing on the bank, someone who can see further down than he can, starts shouting.

teach.b: Hey, the man on the bank calls. You're being carried along by a river that looks pleasant.

teach.h: A POOL WITH WAVES AND WHIRLPOOLS.
teach.b: But downstream there's a pool with waves and whirlpools, with dangerous creatures in it. If you reach it, you'll come to grief.
And the man in the water, hearing that, struggles against the current with his hands and feet. Then the Buddha explains the picture, piece by piece.

The river's current is craving. Its pleasant, alluring look is your own six senses, how good it all seems through them. The pool downstream stands for the five lower fetters, the ties that bind beings to this world.
The waves are anger and despair. The whirlpools are the five strands of sense pleasure, the pull of sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches. Turning against the stream is renunciation.
Struggling with hands and feet is effort.

teach.h: THE ONE ON THE BANK CAN SEE.
teach.b: And the one standing on the bank, who can see what the swimmer can't? That, the Buddha says, is the one who has awakened.

You may remember a swimmer from earlier this year, with four dangers in the water: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, sharks. Today the river adds something: the danger doesn't look dangerous. It looks like a nice afternoon.
In the picture, the whirlpool can't be seen from the water; it takes someone on the bank. And the swimmer in the story hears, and turns.

how: Buddhist teachers often use river and flood images for craving, and some describe the teacher's role, as here, as someone on the bank who can see dangers the practitioner cannot yet see.

o: the current that carries you along
a whirlpool, an eddy in the water
a riverbank where it's safe to stand

games.q: the whirlpool ahead: tap the pairs.
p: the five strands of sense pleasure

s: in the simile the river looks dangerous from the start
it looks lovely and pleasant; that's why the warning is needed.
struggling against the current stands for effort
struggling with hands and feet is effort; turning against the stream is renunciation.
the waves in the pool stand for anger and despair
the Buddha explains each part of the picture.

games.q: you're floating down a lovely river. someone on the bank shouts that there are whirlpools ahead. what does the man in the Itivuttaka do?
o: struggle against the current with hands and feet.
games.why: he hears and turns, working against the current. the Buddha says that struggle is effort, and the one on the bank is the awakened one.

practice: Think of a warning someone has given you lately, gently or not, a friend, a doctor, a parent, even your own body, and picture them on the bank, calling. What can they see that you can't from the water?
You don't have to swim hard yet; just turn your head toward the bank and listen.

wordCard.voice: Avatta, a whirlpool. In the Itivuttaka, a man carried by a pleasant river is warned from the bank of the whirlpools downstream, and turns. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali avatta: a whirlpool, an eddy. in Itivuttaka 109 the whirlpools are the five strands of sense pleasure.

carryVoice: Your line: a stroke toward the bank. The danger in this river looks like a nice afternoon. See you tomorrow.
